storyboard.claim: Gray disguises every act of control as an act of love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's mask — the devoted face over the possessive act.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the reframing mechanism the rest of the segment unpacks.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the disguise as a mask, visualizing the exact mechanism the narration only describes.

storyboard.claim: Gray marks Avery with his own blood instead of naming it as possession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray wiping his blood onto Avery's thigh in the library.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The devotion-language begins with a concrete violating act.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the abstract 'boundary violation' a specific, visible act instead of a summary.

storyboard.claim: He replaces the ownership language with a whispered romantic claim instead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray leaning close, whispering to Avery.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The unspoken possessive line from the previous beat becomes his actual whispered words.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the whisper as intimate framing — the softness that sells the possession.

storyboard.claim: Gray frames total ownership of her body as a shared romantic victory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray holding Avery close, claiming her as territory.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the whispered claim into explicit ownership language.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes 'territory' as physical control rather than letting the romance framing pass uncontested.

storyboard.claim: Avery reads the degrading act as an intimate claiming of shared darkness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery processing what just happened, caught between confusion and yielding.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the framing succeeding — Avery accepting his reinterpretation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes visible that this is Avery's own internal reframe, not a neutral narration claim.

storyboard.claim: Avery explicitly tells herself his control feels like safety.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery alone, her own quoted thought made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Her internal interpretation from the previous beat becomes an explicit direct quote.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts her literal words on screen — the strongest, most direct evidence of the reframe working.

storyboard.claim: The words he uses — mine, protect, claim — exist in healthy romantic devotion too.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery and Gray together, looking like an ordinary romantic couple.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grants the point: this vocabulary is genuinely shared with healthy love.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages them as a plain, unremarkable couple — deliberately ordinary before the next beat's reversal.

storyboard.claim: The same words are also the exact vocabulary of toxic possession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray gripping Avery — the same closeness now read as control.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The identical picture from the previous beat, reread as danger instead of romance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reuses beat 166's staging with a controlling grip — visually proves the vocabulary overlap.

storyboard.claim: Telling healthy devotion from toxic possession takes real critical thinking and objective analysis.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum with the two readings sitting close together, hard to separate.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the previous beat's overlap into an explicit diagram of the ambiguity.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the diagram states the difficulty rather than resolving it — that comes in later beats.

storyboard.claim: Avery's nervous system stays flooded with adrenaline from Lilyale and dopamine from Gray's rewards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery's nervous system depicted as overloaded with reward chemicals.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the reframe works: her body is chemically compromised, not just her judgment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grounds the psychology in physiology instead of leaving 'she can't think straight' vague.

storyboard.claim: When survival and reward chemicals flood the brain, the prefrontal cortex goes offline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow from flooded brain chemistry to logical thought failing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the adrenaline/dopamine flood from the previous beat into its direct mechanical consequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the causal chain explicit rather than just naming the prefrontal cortex.

storyboard.claim: Emotion completely overrides logic — this is a linguistic Trojan horse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery caught in the moment logic loses to feeling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the flow diagram's outcome in the narrator's own words.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: restates the previous beat's diagram in text rather than adding new information.

storyboard.claim: Imagine a stranger on the street stating outright that he intends to control you completely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A menacing figure confronting the viewer-stand-in on the street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the analogy that will reframe everything said so far in plain terms.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the abstract 'boundary violation' into a concrete stranger-danger scenario to judge.

storyboard.claim: The same threat, delivered as a whispered promise to keep you safe, disarms you instead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same man pulling you close and whispering devotion instead of threats.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stranger, opposite tactic — the analogy's turn.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the SAME figure from beat 172 changing tactics, proving it's one strategy, not two people.

storyboard.claim: While he says it, he's quietly locking your front door from the outside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The man locking the door from outside while embracing you.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The whispered safety line from the previous beat now has a literal, trapping action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the metaphor's danger literal and visible — locking a door is unambiguous entrapment.

storyboard.claim: It feels like epic romance, but it's just a prettier cage — and readers fall for it too.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The viewer-stand-in smiling inside a cage they can't see (forced, misplaced happiness).
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what the locked door from the previous beat actually is.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes explicit that the reader, not just Avery, is being fooled — extends the analogy to the audience.

storyboard.claim: Readers fall for the Trojan horse too, hoping Gray really does care in his own way.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in rationalizing Gray's behavior mid-read.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the reader's own hesitation the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the reader's internal excuse-making on screen as a direct, quoted thought.

storyboard.claim: That hesitation is the trap — the book waits for you to step into it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in walking into a narrowing trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the hesitation from the previous beat into the mechanism that catches the reader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the trap as an active structure, not just a metaphorical trap-word.

storyboard.claim: A highwire act of manipulation can't hold forever — an outside force is about to test it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A storm approaching the precarious arrangement between Avery and Gray — Theo is the force about to break it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Signals the trap described in the previous beats is nearing its breaking point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up tension before naming the actual disruptive force in the next beat.

storyboard.claim: Theo is the outside force — the moment his presence starts to crack Gray's mask.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Theo entering the space where Gray has maintained total control.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the outside force the previous beat's 'equilibrium test' referred to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Theo visually as the disruption, ahead of the tattoo scene that follows.

storyboard.claim: Theo, despite being dangerous too, offers Avery a genuine, non-transactional connection Gray never does.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Theo and Avery talking, without the charged control Gray brings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows Theo's entrance with what makes him different from Gray.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the contrast (genuine vs transactional) the tattoo scene will prove.

storyboard.claim: Avery has horrific burn scars on her arm that she hides from everyone, deeply ashamed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Avery pulling her sleeve down over her scarred arm.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the tattoo scene about to happen in what it's covering up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the shame physically (hiding the arm) rather than only stating it.

storyboard.claim: Theo tattoos over her scars carefully, without demanding anything in return or playing mind games.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Theo working the tattoo needle over Avery's scarred arm.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the act that proves what beat 180 promised — a connection with no price.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes 'non-transactional' visible: his hands are occupied with care, not control.

storyboard.claim: The tattoo is an act of reclaiming her bodily autonomy — he never asks her to submit for it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The tattoo taking shape over the scars, Avery watching calmly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the tattoo act, naming its meaning as autonomy rather than submission.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: mostly restates beat 182's staging with the meaning spelled out.

storyboard.claim: This selfless healing contrasts sharply with Gray's transactional approach — and then Gray discovers it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray arriving to find Avery and Theo's connection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts from the healing tattoo scene to the person it threatens.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up his reaction, which the next beats detail.

storyboard.claim: Gray doesn't react with heartbroken jealousy — his reaction is cold, entitled, and terrifying.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's controlled, chilling reaction rather than visible heartbreak.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers what beat 184 set up: not sadness, something colder.
storyboard.addedInformation: Deliberately withholds a 'sad/heartbroken' expression — the negation the narration insists on.

storyboard.claim: He completely loses it, punching a brick wall hard enough to drop chunks of masonry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's fist connecting with a brick wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the physical violence beneath the 'cold and entitled' reaction just named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes his loss of control physically concrete rather than only described.

storyboard.claim: When he confronts Avery, he glares at her with pure hatred, not hurt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's hate-filled glare directed at Avery.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the wall (object) to the confrontation with Avery (person).
storyboard.addedInformation: That distinction — hatred, not hurt — is the beat's whole point, stated directly on screen.

storyboard.claim: He tells her: I told you that you were mine, I did everything right.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray speaking his accusation directly to Avery.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the hateful glare from the previous beat its actual words.
storyboard.addedInformation: Direct quote makes the ownership language explicit rather than inferred.

storyboard.claim: That dialogue completely destroys the constructed persona of the devoted protector.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's composed devoted-protector image collapsing after his own words.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what just happened: his own quote undid the mask built across the whole segment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the turning point — the persona built since beat 160 is now openly broken.

storyboard.claim: Gray's earlier gentleness — tucking her in, soft words — was not selfless love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray tucking Avery into bed, the same tenderness now reread.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reinterprets the earlier tenderness now that the persona has cracked.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reuses the gentle staging, but the strike-through callout tells the viewer it was never what it looked like.

storyboard.claim: He believed he was inserting coins into the Avery vending machine — buying her total submission.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray pulling the lever on a slot machine, mechanizing what he thinks he purchased.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the 'not selfless love' reversal its underlying transactional logic.
storyboard.addedInformation: The slot-machine visual makes 'buying her' a literal mechanism instead of a one-off metaphor.

storyboard.claim: When she connects with Theo, Gray isn't heartbroken over unrequited love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray reacting with cold assertion, not grief.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates the negation from beat 185 now that we know the transactional logic behind it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: largely repeats the 'cold, not sad' point already made at beat 185.

storyboard.claim: He's furious that his property is acting autonomously — which raises a devil's-advocate question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray pointing at Avery as she moves independently of him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the 'not heartbroken' negation with the real emotion: ownership violated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Transitions the segment toward the counterargument the next beats will raise.

storyboard.claim: A devil's-advocate voice argues jealousy is a normal romance trope, like Beauty and the Beast.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader-stand-in making the counterargument aloud.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the pushback against calling Gray's ownership 'property' talk.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the counterargument its own voice rather than folding it into the hosts' commentary.

storyboard.claim: The beast gets possessive and traps her in a castle — and we call that classic romance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray in a controlling stance over Avery, echoing the 'beast traps her' trope.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Illustrates the fictional comparison the devil's advocate just raised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lets the viewer directly compare Gray's control to the genre trope being invoked.

storyboard.claim: Is he a narcissist who views her as property, or just a fiercely protective romantic lead?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray shown ambiguously — the same pose readable both ways.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the actual question underneath the devil's advocate's trope comparison.
storyboard.addedInformation: Poses the distinction as an open question before the next beats resolve it.

storyboard.claim: Normal jealousy is a human emotion; treating a person as a mathematical equation guaranteeing ownership is not.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum separating an ordinary emotion from a calculated exchange.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the open question from the previous beat into the actual distinguishing line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the vague 'crucial distinction' a concrete spectrum instead of leaving it abstract.

storyboard.claim: This isn't romantic jealousy — it's narcissistic injury, and Gray is enraged.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray's controlled fury, now named clinically.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the spectrum from the previous beat with the clinical term.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the psychological diagnosis directly on screen, the segment's key takeaway term.

storyboard.claim: His rage is that of a CEO robbed of a corporate asset, not a man who lost a connection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gray glaring past Avery toward Theo, treating the loss as theft of property, not grief.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the narcissistic-injury diagnosis with the CEO/asset comparison that closes the segment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Points the anger explicitly at Theo (the 'another man') rather than leaving it generic.
